Stamford
STAM-furd
n. (the Lincolnshire stone town of five parish churches, whose Browne's Hospital almshouse of 1475 survived the Reformation and still stands)
Old English Stanford, the stony ford, where the Great North Road crossed the Welland.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Stamford is the Lincolnshire town where the Great North Road crosses the Welland, built throughout of the local limestone, and one of the Five Boroughs of the Danelaw. In the Middle Ages it had fourteen parish churches, five of which survive, four friaries, a Benedictine nunnery and for a brief period in 1333 a breakaway university of seceding Oxford scholars, suppressed by royal writ. Its most instructive survival is Browne's Hospital, founded about 1475 by William Browne, a wool merchant of the Calais staple, as an almshouse for ten poor men and two women with a warden and a confrater; it has a chapel and an audit room and medieval glass, and it has housed poor people continuously for five and a half centuries. Chantries and friaries went at the Reformation; the almshouse, being a charity for the living rather than an endowment for masses for the dead, was kept, reorganised and continued. The dictionary records the distinction as the sharpest practical test of the two religions, since the same merchant's money paid for both, and only one half of it was worth preserving.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an almshouse as a house for the poor; a chantry as an endowment for masses; mercy as tenderness shewn to an offender or sufferer; a warden as a keeper; and afflicted as grieved or distressed.

expand to see more

ALMSHOUSE, n. A house appropriated for the use of the poor; a house maintained by charity.

CHANTRY, n. A church or chapel endowed with lands for the maintenance of priests to sing mass for the souls of the donors.

MERCY, n. That benevolence, mildness or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries, or to treat an offender better than he deserves.

WARDEN, n. A keeper; a guardian; one who has the care or superintendence of a house or institution.

AFFLICTED, a. Affected with continued or often repeated pain; greatly distressed; grieved.

Key Scripture

Hos 6:6 — "For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings."

Mat 23:23 — "Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone."

Zep 3:12 — "I will also leave in the midst of thee an afflicted and poor people, and they shall trust in the name of the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Lincolnshire stone town of the Danelaw with five surviving parish churches, whose Browne's Hospital of about 1475 has housed poor people continuously while its chantries and friaries went at the Reformation.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the chantry again, and Stamford is where the comparison can be made inside one man's will. William Browne, a wool merchant, spent his money on two things: masses for his soul and a house for twelve poor people. The first was swept away at the Reformation and the dictionary counts it a clean gain, since a purchased mass denies the completeness of Christ's one sacrifice and makes the relief of a dead man's estate a matter of coin. The second was kept and has run for five and a half centuries. Hosea states the preference that decides between them in a line: “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings” (Hos 6:6).

The second paragraph guards the judgment from a misuse, because the dictionary is not reducing religion to charity. Our Lord's rebuke to men who tithed herbs and omitted “the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith” (Mat 23:23) is notable for adding that the lesser things ought also to have been done; he is correcting a proportion, not abolishing a duty. What the almshouse witnesses to is the kind of people God has said He will have about Him, “an afflicted and poor people, and they shall trust in the name of the LORD” (Zep 3:12), and the kind of giver He accepts, since “God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble” (Jam 4:6). Fourteen parish churches in one small town is a monument to a religion of multiplied observance; five of them still standing and one almshouse still inhabited is a fair account of what survived the sifting, and the dictionary records that the sifting was done by the right criterion.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chesed (H2617), mercy; Greek barus (G926), weighty; Hebrew 'ani (H6041), afflicted or poor.

expand to see more

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — mercy, kindness, steadfast love; “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice”, Hosea 6:6.

Hebrew da'ath (H1847) — knowledge, perception; “the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings”, Hosea 6:6.

Greek barus (G926) — heavy, weighty; “the weightier matters of the law”, Matthew 23:23.

Greek eleos (G1656) — mercy, compassion; “judgment, mercy, and faith”, Matthew 23:23.

Hebrew 'ani (H6041) — poor, afflicted, humble; “an afflicted and poor people”, Zephaniah 3:12.

Usage

"“For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hos 6:6) — one merchant's masses and one merchant's almshouse."

"“the weightier matters of the law” (Mat 23:23) — a proportion corrected, not a duty abolished."

"“an afflicted and poor people” (Zep 3:12) — twelve poor people housed for five centuries."
